title: Bix, Gatsby, Thomas Wolfe and the American dream in the music
summary: Rose separates Bix from the fictional Gatsby, prefers a comparison to Thomas Wolfe, and says Bix's music, not his life, signifies small-town American dream attitudes; he learned of Bix's life only recently.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: And while the analogies are clear enough there, we have to remember that Bix was a real personality and Gatsby is a fictional one.

I would not make the same analogy between Bix and Fitzgerald, however, even though there were certain superficial similarities, but I don't think that anybody would contend that they were, for artistic purposes, the same. But I would draw your attention to the possibility of making such an analogy, for instance, between Bix and Thomas Wolfe, who fundamentally were from the same origins and developing the same kinds of attitudes and reactions, using similar symbols, although each in a different idiom.

Mm-hmm. Well, I have never, I have not read enough of Thomas Wolfe to know, but I know that you had mentioned that Bix's music conjures up to you the idea of the American dream, something about the American dream. That's right. That's right.
That's right. I mean, the real corner drugstore mom and apple pie attitudes, which were characteristic of his time in America. Now, the music signifies that to you.
The music signifies it. Not Bix's life.
That's right. The music, not the life. And that's where... Actually, I only knew anything at all about Bix's life very recently. I was never interested enough to find out.
All I knew was the music.
